newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end quiet session mixed, techs stumble.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end quiet session mixed, techs stumble.

text.p: Stocks turned in a mixed performance on Friday, with technology stocks suffering heavy losses and blue chips ending little changed.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 4.42 points to close at 6,931.62, down 57.34 points on the week. In the broader market, advancing issues narrowly outpaced declines by 1,270 to 1,210 on active volume of 478 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Weekly volume was 1,967,806,040.

The relative quiet of the broad market masked a tumultuous session for technology stocks, which met with stiff selling. Weakest among blue-chip stocks was International Business Machines Corp., which fell 3-1/2 to 137-3/4.
The pressure was even more severe among semiconductor and networking stocks, as investors stepped back to re-evaulate the formerly high-flying, high-growth sectors.

"People are pulling a little bit off the table here," said Barbara Marcin, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management. "Over the last couple of months, these stocks got a little ahead of themselves."
One problem facing investors is the lack of a convincing reason to commit new money to equities so soon after their torrid January rally, analysts said.

"For too long, markets have been pretty much going straight up," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management Inc. "What's been happening lately is prices have been growing faster than earnings."
Concern about technology's outlook has been particularly sharp because companies in the sector often trade at high earnings multiples, which makes for volatile price swings.
3Com Corp. fell 1-1/2 to 38-5/8 and Cascade Communications Corp. slid 3-1/8 to 25-3/4, as shares in network companies continued to press lower.
The downdraft also drew in industry leader Cisco Systems Inc., which tumbled 4-5/8 to 58-3/8.

While many analysts expect a more challenging stock market over the next couple of months, investors apparently remain committed for the long haul, saying they would be prepared to weather a market correction.

According to a survey released Friday by Nasdaq, 63 percent of investors expect stock prices to rise over the next 12 months and 54 percent would not make major changes to their stock holdings in the event of a significant market decline.
One concern many on Wall Street have expressed is what would occur were stock prices to suffer an extended downturn.

While investors have often asserted their commitment to holding positions for the long term, market observers remain wary, noting the extended bull run has offered little opportunity to test investors' wills.
"Things have been going up so long, people forget markets can go down," Peters said. "That scares me a little."
Among individual issues, Scholastic Corp. shares plummeted 24-3/4, or more than 40 percent, to 36-3/4, a day after warning it would post a fiscal third-quarter loss.
The shares were downgraded by a host of Wall Street firms, with one firm, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, cutting the shares to an outright sell.

Mafco Consolidated Group Inc. rose 4-3/4 to 42 after the company approved a plan to be fully acquired by majority owner Mafco Holdings Inc. Shareholders will get cash payments totalling $43.50 per share in cash under the plan.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 13.08 points to 1,334.32, down 32.87 on the week.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 1.03 points to 801.77, a drop of 6.71 from last Friday. The American Stock Exchange index was off 0.14 at 597.29, down 3.14 on the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.08 to 421.01, down 2.47 from last Friday. The average share lost 1 cent.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,668.963, down 18.283, or 0.24 percent. It fell 68.896 on the week.
